\[
\boxed{\,f(x)=0\ \ (x\ge 0),\qquad f(x)=c\,x\ \ (x<0),\ \text{with an arbitrary constant }c\le 0\,}
\]

**Derivation.**  
Let \(P(x,y)\) denote the assertion.

1. \(P(0,y)\) gives \(y f(0)=2f(0)+f(f(y))\), so \(f(f(y))=f(0)(y-2)\).  
2. \(P(1,y)\) gives \(y f(1)=f(1)+f(f(y))\), so \(f(f(y))=f(1)(y-1)\).  
   Comparing the two affine expressions yields \(f(0)=0\) and hence \(f(f(y))\equiv0\).  
3. \(P(x,0)\) then gives \(0=f(x^2)+f(0)\), so \(f(t)=0\) for all \(t\ge0\).  
4. For \(x\ge0\), the original equation reduces to \(x f(y)+y f(x)=f(xy)\). Since \(f(x)=0\) for \(x\ge0\), for \(x>0\) we get \(f(xy)=x f(y)\).  
5. Taking \(y=-1\) gives \(f(-x)=x f(-1)\) for all \(x>0\); thus for \(t<0\), \(f(t)=c t\) with \(c=-f(-1)\).  
6. The condition \(f(f(y))=0\) forces \(c\le0\) (if \(c>0\) then \(f(f(-1))=c^2(-1)\ne0\)).  
7. Direct substitution shows every such function satisfies the equation.

\[
\boxed{f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\ge 0,\\ c\,x,&x<0,\end{cases}\qquad\text{where }c\le 0\text{ is an arbitrary constant.}}
\]

Equivalently \(f(x)=k\max\{-x,0\}\) for any \(k\ge 0\).

**Derivation.** Let \(P(x,y)\) denote the given assertion.

- \(P(0,y):\; yf(0)=2f(0)+f(f(y))\).  
- \(P(1,y):\; f(y)+yf(1)=f(y)+f(1)+f(f(y))\), hence \(f(f(y))=f(1)y-f(1)\).

Comparing the two expressions for \(f(f(y))\) gives \(f(0)=f(1)\) and \(2f(0)=f(1)\), so \(f(0)=f(1)=0\). Then \(f(f(y))\equiv0\).

- \(P(x,0):\; 0=f(0)+f(x^2)+f(f(0))=f(x^2)\), so \(f(t)=0\) for all \(t\ge0\).

Substituting these into the original equation yields the reduced identity
\[
|x|f(y)+yf(x)=f(xy)\qquad(\ast).
\]

- \(P(x,-1)\) in \((\ast)\): \(|x|f(-1)-f(x)=f(-x)\). For \(x\ge0\) we have \(f(x)=0\), so \(f(-x)=x f(-1)\). Writing \(z=-x\le0\) and \(c=-f(-1)\), we obtain
\[
f(z)=cz\ \ (z\le0),\qquad f(z)=0\ \ (z\ge0).
\]

Finally, the condition \(f(f(y))=0\) forces, for \(y<0\), that \(f(cy)=0\). Since \(y<0\), \(cy\ge0\) exactly when \(c\le0\). Thus \(c\le0\).

Conversely, every function of this form satisfies \(f\equiv0\) on \([0,\infty)\), \(f(f(y))=0\), and a direct case check of signs verifies \((\ast)\) (and hence the original equation) for any \(c\le0\).
